pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural fluency of moving both ways between decimal notation and tenths/hundredths fractions: read 0.62 as 62/100, write 3/10 as 0.3, read 0.07 as 7/100, and locate them on a number line. It rests on the place-value meaning that the first place after the point is tenths and the second is hundredths, so the number of decimal places is governed by the denominator (10 → one place, 100 → two places) and a placeholder zero is required when the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros (7/100 = 0.07). The skill is assessed by WATCHING the child convert both directions, especially on the placeholder cases that a digit-copying rule gets wrong.
bestPractices: Practise BOTH directions from the start (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) using a place-value chart so the child reads the denominator off the final place.
Foreground the placeholder: pair 3/10 = 0.3 with 7/100 = 0.07 and 3/100 = 0.03 so the child learns that hundredths always occupy two places and a zero holds an empty tenths place.
Link every conversion to a picture — a hundredths grid and a number-line location — so the symbolic answer is checked against a quantity, catching reversals like 0.62 → 6/2.
Use ragged and single-digit-numerator cases deliberately (0.4, 0.07, 9/100) because these are where the placeholder rule bites and hollow digit-copying fails.
Have the child read the decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside the fraction
10×10 hundredths grid shaded to match the decimal and the fraction
Contrasting sets {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07} to drill the placeholder
Bidirectional conversion cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other)
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero: writing 9/100 as 0.9, or reading 0.07 as 7/10.
Adding an unneeded zero: writing 3/10 as 0.03 by over-applying 'hundredths = two places'.
Using one denominator for every decimal: writing 0.4 as 4/100 regardless of the number of places.
Reversing digits or reading position wrong: 0.62 → 6/2 or 26/100.
Placing decimals on the number line by whole-number reasoning rather than by tenths/hundredths.

learn.summary: Learners move fluently in BOTH directions between decimal notation and tenths/hundredths fractions: read 0.62 as 62/100, write 3/10 as 0.3, read 0.07 as 7/100, and locate these on a 0–1 number line. The skill rests on place-value meaning — the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths — so the denominator is read from the final place (10 → one place, 100 → two places), and a placeholder zero is needed when the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros (7/100 = 0.07). Learning and checking should deliberately use placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases, because a digit-copying rule produces correct answers on easy items but fails exactly there.

activities.title: Two-way converter checked against a grid and a number line
feedback: If a learner writes 0.9 for 9/100, point to the grid: ninety squares versus nine. The nine belongs in the hundredths (second) place, so a zero holds the empty tenths place — contrast 9/10 = 0.9 with 9/100 = 0.09.
If a learner writes 0.4 as 4/100, read the final place aloud: 0.4 ends in the tenths place, so it is 4/10 (or equivalently 40/100). Shade 4 columns versus 4 single squares to contrast.

If a learner over-applies 'hundredths means two places' and writes 3/10 as 0.03, contrast 3/10 = 0.3 (one place) with 3/100 = 0.03 (two places): a placeholder is needed only when the denominator has more zeros than the numerator has digits.
If a learner reverses digits (0.62 → 26/100) or loses the place value (0.62 → 6/2), use the place-value chart to name each digit's place before writing the fraction.
activities.rationale: Bidirectional conversion is a doing-skill, so the learner should produce many items with immediate quantity-based feedback rather than only reading a worked rule. Linking symbol, grid and number line lets placeholder errors show as mismatched pictures, turning a rote rule into a self-correcting action. Deliberately including placeholder and ragged cases targets exactly where digit-copying fails. Live grid shading and the number-line marker are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; a paper hundredths grid and a drawn number line serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal notation stem largely from false analogies with whole numbers and incomplete place-value understanding; because faulty digit-based rules can produce correct answers on easy items, instruction and assessment must use cases (single-digit numerators, ragged decimals) that expose the placeholder and place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Enter a decimal (e.g. 0.62) and write the matching fraction; confirm against a 10×10 hundredths grid that shades 62 squares and a number-line marker that lands just past halfway.
Enter a fraction (e.g. 3/10) and write the matching decimal (0.3); confirm by shading 3 of the ten columns and placing the point on the line.
Do the hard placeholder case: for 9/100, if you write 0.9 the grid floods with ninety squares — far more than nine — so the mismatch is obvious; correct it to 0.09 so exactly nine squares glow.
Run rapid two-way rounds (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) across a deliberate set of placeholder and ragged cases: 0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100.
Read each decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths', 'seven hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
activities.intendedInsight: The placeholder zero is not a rule to memorise but something you can see: for 9/100 the zero keeps the nine out of the tenths place. The denominator is determined by the final decimal place, and every symbolic answer can be checked against a shaded quantity and a position on the line.

activities.title: Contrast sets that drill the placeholder
feedback: If a learner treats 3/10 and 3/100 as the same, compare the two shaded grids directly — the quantities are visibly different.
If a learner uses one denominator for every decimal, have them name the final place of each decimal aloud before choosing the denominator.
activities.rationale: Deliberately pairing ragged and single-digit-numerator cases targets exactly where digit-copying fails, as the decimal-research-based source recommends. Contrasting cards (decimal one side, fraction the other) support self-checking without requiring any particular device.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal notation stem largely from false analogies with whole numbers and incomplete place-value understanding; because faulty digit-based rules can produce correct answers on easy items, instruction and assessment must use cases (single-digit numerators, ragged decimals) that expose the placeholder and place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Work matched pairs side by side: {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07}, writing each as both a fraction and a decimal.
For each pair, shade a hundredths grid for both members so the size difference is visible (3 columns vs 3 squares; 70 squares vs 7 squares).
State in words why one needs a placeholder zero and the other does not.
Sort a mixed set of cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other) and self-check by flipping, giving special attention to 0.4, 0.07 and 9/100.
activities.intendedInsight: Tenths and hundredths of the same digit look similar in writing but differ ten-fold in size; the number of decimal places and the presence of a placeholder zero both follow from which place the final digit occupies.

activities.title: Annotated place-value chart as a reference (scaffold)
feedback: After reading, ask the learner to convert a fresh placeholder case unaided (e.g. 0.07 → 7/100) and explain each step in place-value terms.
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart can present the rule and worked examples as a reference, which supports learners who need the method spelled out. It is a scaffold: on its own it does not provide the repeated production-with-feedback that builds conversion fluency, so it should lead back into active conversion.
learnerActions: Study a place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside a couple of worked conversions, e.g. 0.62 = 62/100 and 9/100 = 0.09.
Read a short explanation of why the placeholder zero appears in 0.09 but not in 0.3.
Return to the converter or contrast-set tasks and reproduce the method on new values without looking.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked reference makes the place–denominator link and the placeholder rule explicit, but fluency comes from doing many items, not from reading examples.

constraints: Practise both directions (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) from the start; a learner may be fluent one way but not the other.
Deliberately include placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases (0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100): easy items can be answered correctly by digit-copying and so do not reveal understanding.
Correct answers: 0.62 = 62/100; 0.07 = 7/100; 0.4 = 4/10 (equivalently 40/100); 3/10 = 0.3; 9/100 = 0.09; 0.03 = 3/100; 0.4 sits at four tenths, just below halfway on a 0–1 line.
Check every conversion against a quantity (shaded grid) and a position (number line) to catch place-value errors such as 0.62 → 6/2 (dropping the place value) or 0.62 → 26/100 (reversing digits).
The annotated chart is a reference scaffold, not a substitute for repeated production with feedback.
Fixed worked examples can still teach the method; they simply cannot be manipulated, so pair them with learner-generated items.

A scored check can be used during teaching to surface errors, but on its own it measures the skill more than it builds it; use its placeholder distractors (e.g. 0.9 for 9/100, 7/10 for 0.07) diagnostically.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source national-curriculum claim is marked verified:false in the original row and supports the topic/statutory requirement rather than any activity's teaching principle; it was therefore not retained as an activity sourceClaim. It remains relevant as age-appropriate curriculum context (Year 4, ages 9–10): pupils should recognise and write decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.

The original artefact ratings asserted that 3D 'adds no conceptual value', that a character/dialogue format 'adds nothing', and that assessment-format steps 'do not build' the skill. These are catalog-preference judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped statements about affordances or omitted as universal claims.
No arithmetic or place-value error was found in the source conversions; all stated conversions (0.62=62/100, 0.07=7/100, 0.4=4/10, 3/10=0.3, 9/100=0.09, 3/100=0.03) are correct and retained.

probeDeeper: You wrote 0.07 = 7/100. What would 0.7 be instead — and how do the two differ in size?
How did you decide 0.4 is 4/10 and not 4/100? What tells you the denominator?
Where does 0.4 sit relative to a half on this line — and how do you know without measuring?
A friend writes 3/10 as 0.03. Is that right? If not, what is 0.03 as a fraction?

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero — reads 0.07 as 7/10, or writes 9/100 as 0.9 — mapping the digit straight after the point.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart / grid: the 9 belongs in the hundredths (second) place, so a zero holds the tenths place; contrast 9/10 = 0.9 with 9/100 = 0.09. Reteach that place fixes the denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forces one denominator on every decimal — writes 0.4 as 4/100 (or 40/1000), ignoring the number of places.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the final place aloud: 0.4 ends in the tenths place, so 4/10; shade 4 columns vs 4 squares to contrast. Reteach reading the denominator from the last place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 0.4 → 4/100; treats every decimal as hundredths regardless of length.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds an unneeded zero — over-applies 'hundredths means two places' and writes 3/10 as 0.03.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 3/10 = 0.3 (one place) with 3/100 = 0.03 (two places) on the chart; the placeholder is needed only when the denominator has more zeros than the numerator has digits. Reteach the place–denominator link.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3/10 → 0.03; inserts a placeholder where none is needed.

responseLevels.gap: Converts by copying digits regardless of place (0.07 → 7/10, 0.4 → 4/100), reverses digits, or places 0.4 by whole-number reasoning. No reliable link to place value.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions accurately including placeholder cases (0.07 = 7/100, 9/100 = 0.09), chooses the denominator from the final place (0.4 = 4/10), locates 0.4 correctly on the line, and explains each step in place-value terms; transfers to new values.
responseLevels.partial: Converts tenths and most hundredths correctly but slips on placeholder cases (0.07, 9/100) or on choosing the denominator (0.4), or converts fluently one way but not the other; can execute without explaining the place–denominator link.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write these decimals as fractions: 0.62, 0.07, 0.4. Now write these as decimals: 3/10, 9/100. Last, mark 0.4 on this number line from 0 to 1. Show me how you work each one out.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the work separates place-value understanding from digit-copying. The 0.07 and 9/100 items are placeholder discriminators — a hollow rule yields 7/10 and 0.9. The 0.4 item checks whether the child forces every decimal to hundredths (4/100) or reads the place. Doing both directions and locating on the line exposes reversals and whole-number placement that a one-way written check would miss.
